extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, legal scholars, law students, and policymakers interested in patent subject-matter eligibility
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and doctrinal criteria for assessing whether inventions meet statutory subject-matter limits (§101) and related doctrines (Mayo/Alice, EPO technicality, §112 enablement/written description), illustrated with software, diagnostics, and gene-patent examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory categories of patentable subject matter (§101)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 101 defines patentable subject matter as new and useful processes, machines, compositions of matter, or articles of manufacture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes product patents (machines, compositions, manufactures — usually tangible) from process patents (characterized by sets of relationships between tangible entities). Use the statutory categories as the starting point for eligibility analysis and recognize how process vs product descriptions affect characterization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusions from patentable subject matter (laws of nature, abstract ideas, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Doctrinal exclusions include laws of nature, abstract ideas, mental steps, symbolic indicia, discoveries, scientific theories, mathematical methods, aesthetic creations, rules/methods for mental acts, methods for playing games or doing business, computer programs, and presentations of information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These categories overlap heavily and travel together; determining which exclusion applies can be difficult because reframing an invention slightly can move it from one exclusion (e.g., abstract idea) to another (e.g., law of nature).

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine-or-transformation test
rubrics_metrics.description: A process may be patent-eligible if it is tied to a machine or effects a transformation of matter — the 'machine or transformation' test developed by the Federal Circuit and discussed by the Supreme Court in Bilski.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bilski held this is a possible subject-matter test but not the sole determinant; reliance on the test risks excluding modern software and diagnostic inventions that do not neatly exhibit material transformations.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPO 'technical' requirement / technical contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: The European Patent Office (EPO) concluded the common feature among many exclusions is a 'substantial lack of technical character' and historically searched for 'technical character' or 'technical contribution.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term 'technical' proved elusive. More recent EPO practice treats recitation of any physical apparatus as sufficient to render claims technical, leaving invalidation to novelty/inventive step. This approach shows one way to treat borderline claims (e.g., software).

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical instantiation / materiality to avoid exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims tied to physical apparatus, circuits, storage devices, or other material substrates are more likely to avoid being characterized as abstract ideas or laws of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Software and symbolic representations often collapse into physical instantiations (e.g., voltages in a circuit). Drafting that ties a claim to concrete substrates can make it more likely to be viewed as patent-eligible, although the Supreme Court warns against eligibility depending solely on drafting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement and written description (§112) — commensurability principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 112(a) requires disclosure enabling one of ordinary skill to make and use the claimed invention and a description sufficient to show possession; the disclosure must be commensurate with claim scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A patentee who wants to claim more must disclose more; §112 can constrain overbroad claims and functions as a practical limit on claim breadth (potentially obviating the need for additional §101 limits). This is especially important for claims that purport to cover mental steps or general principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drafting to apparatus/product versus abstract process ('doctrine of the magic words')
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants often draft process claims as apparatus or product claims—describing the apparatus or substrates involved—to lend tangibility to otherwise abstract inventions (what Lemley and Cohen call the 'doctrine of the magic words').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such drafting can circumvent some subject-matter exclusions, but the Supreme Court has disfavored eligibility turning solely on crafty drafting. Nevertheless, both US and EPO practice show that reciting physical instantiation can influence eligibility and downstream validity analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-step Mayo/Alice subject-matter test (building blocks + inventive concept)
rubrics_metrics.description: First ask whether the claimed invention is directed to a 'building block' category (abstract idea, law of nature, product of nature). If so, ask whether the claim adds an 'inventive concept' sufficient to transform the ineligible concept into patent-eligible application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The addition of 'insignificant postsolution activity' is not enough. The 'inventive concept' must be more than conventional activity and must meaningfully limit the claim beyond the building block.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preemption / breadth as an indicator of problematic claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that would 'preempt' fundamental building blocks or large swaths of future innovation are disfavored; the tendency to preempt is treated as a marker of problematic subject-matter claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preemption is not always the justificatory basis but is used diagnostically: claims of a type that typically preempt future innovation are likely to be excluded. Narrowing claims to particular instantiations or apparatuses reduces preemption concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Processes as inherently involving natural laws and substrate relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: All processes entail causal relationships among substrates that follow natural laws; processes are described by relationships among material entities and so implicate laws-of-nature exclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because all processes reflect causal order, eligibility often turns on how the process is described (in terms of human artifacts or in terms of correlations/principles). Characterizing substrates as human artifacts (machines, manufactures) helps avoid 'natural' labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claiming mental steps and abstract reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that encompass purely mental processes or 'comparing'/'analyzing' steps (abstract mental steps) are likely to be held ineligible under Mayo/Alice reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagnostic methods and other deductive processes are at risk because diagnosis is fundamentally a process of deduction using natural correlations. Courts have viewed 'comparing' sequence claims as claiming a natural correlation or an abstract mental step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insignificant post-solution activity is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding routine or conventional stages (insignificant postsolution activity) to an otherwise abstract claim does not render it patent-eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drafting must add more than trivial implementation steps to survive the second step of Alice/Mayo; courts will look for meaningful inventive contribution beyond the abstract idea or natural principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of relying on drafting skill for eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court has warned that patent eligibility should not depend on the 'skill of the draftsman'—i.e., clever claim-drafting should not determine eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Despite the admonition, jurisprudence (and EPO practice) has often led patentees to attempt to escape exclusions via drafting. Courts face tension between discouraging reliance on drafting and allowing narrow concrete claims to pass muster.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of novelty and inventive step / non-obviousness to police borderline subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Other doctrines like novelty and inventive step (non-obviousness) and novelty-based invalidity are used to weed out dubious claims that have been made technically eligible by reciting physical instantiation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPO and some US approaches accept claims tied to physical instantiation but then filter them on novelty/inventive step grounds; this provides an alternate enforcement mechanism when §101 is permissive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interplay between product and process claims (Durden problem)
rubrics_metrics.description: New materials (products) and new relationships (processes) often give rise to interlocking product and process claims; the allocation of patentability between them is complex (the 'Durden' problem).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patentees commonly draft both product and process claims; courts and doctrine (e.g., product-by-process enforcement rules) affect how such claims are treated for infringement and validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic method eligibility tension (Myriad/Mayo precedent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Diagnostic process claims that claim correlations between biological sequences/markers and disease risk are likely to be viewed as claiming natural correlations and thus ineligible under Mayo; yet the Supreme Court suggested methods of manipulating genes or applications of knowledge might be permissible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is tension between lower-court unanimity rejecting diagnostic claims and Supreme Court dicta suggesting some process claims involving genes might be allowed. Practitioners must carefully frame diagnostic claims to avoid claiming mere correlations or mental steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commensurability as a practical limit on claim breadth
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle that a patentee may only claim what she teaches (commensurability) limits claim breadth and addresses concerns about overbroad claims that claim fundamental principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applying §112's requirement that disclosure match claimed scope can serve as an effective check on preemption and may reduce the need for an expansive §101 exclusion aimed at breadth control.
